newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Peronists plan new Ethics Office, opposition scoffs.
newsitem.headline: Peronists plan new Ethics Office, opposition scoffs.

text.p: The Argentine government on Wednesday hailed plans for a new "Ethics Office" as a boost for democracy and economic growth, but the opposition scoffed at the idea of the ruling Peronists fighting corruption.

President Carlos Menem, whose government has been plagued with corruption scandals since he came to power in 1989, returned from meeting U.S. President Bill Clinton last week with plans for a U.S.-style Office of Public Ethics.

Interior Minister Carlos Corach, opening a government-sponsored seminar on public ethics, said the new watchdog "will not investigate cases of corruption, but give advice and orientation to officials and agencies on the ethical behaviour they should follow."
Economy Minister Roque Fernandez told the seminar: "There is no growth for all without ethics ... the real cause of the growth crisis we suffered for decades."

There was also advice from attendee Stephen Potts, head of the U.S. Public Ethics Office. He addressed a common concern of local and foreign business by telling Pagina 12 newspaper it was vital "to have a brave, independent court system to prove corruption cases and punish the criminals."

Corruption among public officials and the suspicion of cover-ups in the courts has put been in the spotlight lately by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, who has been on a campaign against graft since being sacked by Menem in July.

He has accused Corach, Justice Minister Elias Jassan and Menem's Chief of Staff Alberto Kohan of covering up graft or manipulating judges, and said two Supreme Court judges are "corrupt thieves." Corach and a judge are suing Cavallo.
Cavallo has also called Fernandez "dishonest or not capable" for condoning a businessman he accuses of graft.

From the political opposition, the leader of the Frepaso centre-left coalition Carlos "Chacho" Alvarez scorned the idea of an Ethics Office set up by the Peronists, saying "they would have to fight themselves" if they fought corruption.

Former President Raul Alfonsin of the Radical Party said ethical behaviour in public office "is not an ideological problem, simply a problem of honesty," and Radical economist Ricardo Lopez Murphy said he backed the plan as long as it was headed "by someone who is not a friend of the government."
There was outspoken praise for Menem's record on graft from outgoing U.S. Ambassador James Cheek, who said on Tuesday he had not seen one case of corruption in 3-1/2 years here.
But major corruption cases involving Argentine officials and private companies are constantly in the news.

U.S. computer giant International Business Machines' local unit is under investigation for alleged bribery and customs officials are being questioned about a "parallel customs" ring suspected of smuggling in $10 billion of goods in four years.
